title: Nginx Reverse Proxy Buffer Overflow and Upstream Load Shedding
subtitle: Client Body Buffer Tuning, Disk Spooling Penalties and Zero-Copy TCP Optimization
problem_statement: An API Gateway using Nginx in front of Python/Java microservices handles 2,000 RPS. When mobile clients on slow 3G connections request 2MB JSON reports, upstream app server workers remain blocked for 15+ seconds per client because proxy buffering was disabled to 'save memory', exhausting application worker threads.

faded_bug.description: proxy_buffering off causes upstream app workers to be tied to client transmission speed (Slowloris effect).

invariants.description: Upstream application workers must not exceed 80% saturation due to slow client reads.

probing_ladder.stage_1_validation: Explain how epoll in Nginx decouples client socket reads from upstream keepalive TCP connections.
probing_ladder.stage_2_tightening: If proxy_buffering is ON and the response size is 50MB, what does Nginx do when proxy_buffers are filled? What is the impact on NVMe drive lifespan?
probing_ladder.stage_3_adversarial: An attacker sends HTTP POST requests with Content-Length 1000000 at 1 byte every 10 seconds. How does your reverse proxy protect the upstream services?
probing_ladder.stage_4_squeeze: How do you configure zero-copy transfer (`sendfile` and `tcp_nopush`) for static assets to bypass user-space memory copies?

counter_probes.counter_question: If the issue is slow TCP window draining by client cellular networks, scaling upstream app pods costs $5,000/month in idle JVMs. Why not let Nginx buffer the payload in RAM in 2ms?
counter_probes.expected_staff_answer: Proxy buffering allows the upstream application to complete in 2ms and return to the pool, while Nginx handles the slow 10-second client drain with negligible kernel memory.
